prewrittenContent.hook: 5 things that make a contractor website look abandoned
prewrittenContent.body:
Slide 1: 5 things that make a contractor website look abandoned
Slide 2: No phone number above the fold. If someone has to hunt for it, they call the next name instead.
Slide 3: A contact form and nothing else. No phone, no way to just call — a website's whole job is to make it easy.
Slide 4: Stock photos of a crew that clearly isn't the crew. It reads as fake before anyone reads a word of copy.
Slide 5: No reviews visible anywhere. If the trust is there, the site should show it, not hide it.
Slide 6: A site that hasn't changed in years. It signals the business might not be either. We build sites that don't do any of this.

prewrittenContent.hook: Your next customer already searched for you today.
prewrittenContent.body:
Your next customer already searched for you today.

They had a job that needed doing. They picked up their phone and searched for someone in your trade.

A few names came up. If yours wasn't one of them, you didn't lose that job — you never knew it existed.

No missed call. No message to follow up on. Just a customer who called someone else and a workday that looked completely normal.

That's the part that's easy to miss. The losses that don't announce themselves.

Save this if it sounds familiar.

— Trevo

Here's what's inside a Trevo plumbing site.

Tap-to-call button, visible on every page, one thumb reach.
Service pages built for the jobs that actually pay — drain clearing, water heaters, leak repair, emergency calls.
Google reviews pulled in automatically, so trust is visible before anyone has to ask for it.
Licensed and insured status shown clearly, not buried in a footer.
Mobile-first layout, because most of this traffic is a phone.

That's the build. — Trevo
